summary: This Wikipedia article explains radicals in chemistry: atoms, molecules, or ions with at least one unpaired valence electron, which makes them highly reactive. It covers how radicals form (homolysis, reduction, abstraction, addition, elimination), what stabilizes organic and inorganic radicals, diradicals such as oxygen, and their roles in combustion, polymerization, atmospheric chemistry, and biology, including reactive oxygen species. It also covers the history and nomenclature of the term, and how radicals are depicted in reactions.
one_line: Overview of chemical radicals: species with unpaired valence electrons, their formation, stability, occurrence in combustion, atmosphere and biology, and history.
key_facts: A radical, also known as a free radical, is an atom, molecule, or ion that has at least one unpaired valence electron.
The hydroxyl radical (HO·) has one unpaired electron on the oxygen atom.
Triplet oxygen and triplet carbene (:CH2) are two examples of species with two unpaired electrons.
Homolysis makes two new radicals from a spin-paired molecule by breaking a covalent bond, and it requires energy from heat or light.
Splitting H2 into 2 H• requires a ΔH° of +435 kJ/mol, while splitting Cl2 into two Cl• requires a ΔH° of +243 kJ/mol.
Tertiary carbon radicals are the most stable and primary radicals the least stable, because of hyperconjugation with adjacent C-H bonds.
TEMPO, or (2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxyl, is stable enough to be sold commercially in its radical form because steric hindrance from its four methyl groups prevents reaction.
Alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) is a highly effective hydrogen-atom donor that functions as an antioxidant.
Moses Gomberg discovered the triphenylmethyl radical, (C6H5)3C•, in 1900, the first organic radical identified in a modern context.
Louis-Bernard Guyton de Morveau introduced the phrase "radical" in 1785, and Antoine Lavoisier employed it in 1789 in his Traité Élémentaire de Chimie.
In 1933 Morris S. Kharasch and Frank Mayo proposed that free radicals were responsible for anti-Markovnikov addition of hydrogen bromide to allyl bromide.
Gerhard Herzberg suggested a looser definition of free radicals as "any transient (chemically unstable) species (atom, molecule, or ion)".
Because lead deactivates radicals in the gasoline-air mixture, tetraethyl lead was once commonly added to gasoline.
The photodissociation of chlorofluorocarbons by solar ultraviolet radiation produces chlorine radicals, which catalyze the conversion of ozone to O2 and cause ozone depletion.
Methyl methacrylate (MMA) can be polymerized by radical addition steps to produce poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA, Plexiglas or Perspex).
